entity.name: Benjamin Franklin
entity.description: The runaway apprentice who became America's most versatile founding father. Printer, scientist, inventor, diplomat -- the only person to sign the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution. Flew a kite in a thunderstorm, charmed the French court, and still signed his letters 'B. Franklin, Printer.'

story.name: Benjamin Franklin
story.description: Runs away from Boston at 17, flies a kite in a lightning storm, secures France's alliance for the Revolution, and signs three of America's founding documents. The original American self-made man.

moments.name: Benjamin Franklin Is Born the 15th of 17 Children on Milk Street
moments.subtitle: The son of a candle maker who will become the most accomplished American of his century
moments.description: On January 17, 1706, Benjamin Franklin was born on Milk Street in Boston, Province of Massachusetts Bay. His father Josiah, a tallow chandler and soap maker who had emigrated from England, had 17 children by two wives; Benjamin was the 15th child and the youngest son. Josiah wanted Benjamin to enter the clergy but could only afford two years of schooling. At age 12, Benjamin became an apprentice to his older brother James, a printer. Franklin's formal education ended at age ten, but he became one of the most voracious readers and prolific writers in colonial America, eventually earning honorary degrees from Harvard, Yale, and Oxford.

moments.name: A 17-Year-Old Franklin Runs Away to Philadelphia with Almost Nothing
moments.subtitle: A fugitive apprentice walks into the city that will make him famous, clutching three puffy rolls
moments.description: In 1723, 17-year-old Benjamin Franklin fled Boston for Philadelphia, abandoning his apprenticeship to his brother James without permission, which technically made him a fugitive. He arrived in Philadelphia nearly penniless, famously walking through the streets eating one of three large puffy rolls he had purchased. Franklin soon found work in several printing shops. The city was the largest and most cosmopolitan in the colonies. Within six years, Franklin would own The Pennsylvania Gazette and begin his rise as colonial America's most prominent citizen. His autobiography immortalized this arrival as the archetypal American self-reinvention story.

moments.name: Franklin Flies a Kite in a Thunderstorm and Proves Lightning Is Electrical
moments.subtitle: A printer-turned-scientist risks electrocution to change the history of physics
moments.description: In June 1752, Benjamin Franklin conducted his famous kite experiment in Philadelphia, proving that lightning was electrical in nature. Franklin flew a kite with a metal key attached to the string during a thunderstorm and observed electrical sparks jumping from the key. The experiment confirmed his hypothesis and led directly to his invention of the lightning rod, which could protect buildings from lightning strikes. The discovery made Franklin internationally famous and earned him the Royal Society's Copley Medal. It was one of the most important experiments of the 18th century and made Franklin a major figure in the history of physics.

moments.name: Franklin Secures the French Alliance That Saves the American Revolution
moments.subtitle: A 70-year-old in a fur cap charms Versailles into bankrolling a rebellion across the ocean
moments.description: On February 6, 1778, Benjamin Franklin, serving as the first American ambassador to France, signed the Treaty of Alliance with France in Paris. Franklin had arrived in December 1776, at age 70, and became a sensation in French high society, cultivating an image as a rustic American philosopher. His diplomatic skill was critical: France agreed to provide military support, naval power, and financial aid to the American colonies in their war against Britain. French assistance proved decisive. The alliance led to France sending troops and a fleet that helped win the Battle of Yorktown in 1781, effectively ending the Revolutionary War.

moments.name: Benjamin Franklin Dies at 84 as 20,000 Attend His Funeral
moments.subtitle: The man on the hundred-dollar bill leaves a will that funds scholarships for 200 years
moments.description: On April 17, 1790, Benjamin Franklin died at his home in Philadelphia at the age of 84. An estimated 20,000 people attended his funeral, the largest gathering Philadelphia had ever seen. Franklin was the only person to have signed all three of America's founding documents: the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris, and the Constitution. In his will, he left 1,000 pounds each to Boston and Philadelphia in trust, to be loaned to young tradesmen at interest for 200 years. When the trusts matured in 1990, they had grown to millions of dollars. He remains one of the most honored Americans, his face on the $100 bill.
